open_questions: Depth 35% change between 2 sectors and p_consistent 0.025091 — spot evolution vs systematic aperture/QLP; needs additional TESS or ground photometry to stabilize depth.
Low SNR 15.62 with only 3 transits, 0.3639 share in one season — need more transits for period confirmation and achromatic depth check.
star ruwe 1.222 and VARIABLE flag — Gaia binary check inconclusive; RV mass measurement needed to rule out low-mass stellar companion with flat eclipse.
dossier.public_summary: A small, flat-bottomed 5-hour dip repeats every 13.5 days on a nearby K dwarf, with a size equivalent to about 4 Earth radii and no sign of a second eclipse or odd-even difference. The dip looks shallow in one sector and deeper in another and comes from only three events so far, likely because of the star's own spot activity and TESS's limited signal, but there is no nearby star that could cause it and no evidence for a binary. More transits and follow-up will confirm the period and rule out a small star, but a planet is the best fit now.

reasons.why: Strongly flat-bottomed box transit, not V-shaped grazing EB, despite 1.44 duration ratio which stellar_radius tool shows implies 3.93 Rearth (TIC) / 3.72-3.77 Rearth (Gaia FLAME/GSP-Phot) — all sub-giant, consistent with planet.
Undiluted depth still planet-sized N3.9, well below stellar 10-22+ Re threshold; duration fits central duration 3.471h with modest b=0.07961, star_density_penalty -0.5329.
No significant odd/even difference and no secondary at snr >=5 or distinct from spot brightening; argues against EB at 13.5d or 27d.

reasons.why: Depth does vary 1984 ppm (sector 58) to 2840 ppm (sector 86) and per-transit p=0.025, consistent with low-SNR 3-transit (2.4-min period star, 43% share) systematics/spot contamination, but all sectors flat-bottomed and no plausible neighbour inside 1px (plausible_within_1px 0, closest that could 16 arcsec delta_mag 5.36). No centroid off-target evidence; best explanation is planet on target with stellar activity, similar TESS planets exist.
